(CNN)  -- A suburban Philadelphia swim club has invited children from a largely minority day-care center to come back after a June reversal that fueled allegations of racism against the club, a spokeswoman said Sunday. Some kids from the Creative Steps Day Care center say club members made racial remarks. The development came during a hastily called Sunday afternoon meeting of the Valley Club in Huntingdon Valley, Pennsylvania. Club members voted overwhelmingly to try to work things out with the day-care center, which accused some swim club members of making racist comments to black and Hispanic children contracted to use the pool, said Bernice Duesler, the club director's wife. Duesler said the club canceled its contract with the Creative Steps day-care because of safety, crowding and noise concerns, not racism. "As long as we can work out safety issues, we'd like to have them back," she told CNN. She said the club has been subpoenaed by the state Human Rights Commission, which has begun a fact-finding investigation, "and the legal advice was to try to get together with these camps, " Duesler added. Alethea Wright, Creative Steps' director, said, "They should have done that before." Wright has repeatedly lambasted the club for its tepid response to the charges and said the children in her care were "emotionally damaged" by the incident. "These children are scarred. How can I take those children back there?" she said. However, Wright's lawyer, Carolyn Nicholas, said the center will give the Valley Club's offer "due consideration" once it is received and looks forward to sitting down with the parties. "The children are our primary concern," Nicholas told CNN. Swimming privileges for about 65 children from Creative Steps were revoked after their first visit June 29. Some children said white members of the club made racist comments to the children, asking why "black children were there" and raising concerns that "they might steal from us." Days later, the day-care center's $1,950 check was returned, Wright said. Club director John Duesler told CNN that he had underestimated the amount of children who would participate, and the club was unable to supervise that many kids. He called his club "very diverse," and said it had offered to let day camps in the Philadelphia area use his facility after budget cuts forced some pools in the area to close. Wright has rejected the camp's contention that the swim club's pool was overcrowded. The club had accepted a 10-to-1 ratio of children to adults and was considering adding up to three lifeguards, according to e-mails obtained by CNN. But John Duesler said last week that the Valley Club also canceled contracts with two other day-care centers because of safety and overcrowding issues. The Pennsylvania Human Rights Commission launched an investigation last week after allegations of racism at the Valley Club. The commission said that as part of any investigation, the two sides eventually could be asked to sit down face-to-face with its investigators. "We always encourage opposing parties to communicate with one another if they feel they can resolve these issues amicably," Commission Chairman Stephen Glassman said. Bernice Duesler said she wasn't yet sure how the club will "reach out" to Creative Steps and the other two camps. And Wright said she still has concerns about the issue. "Are the members who made those comments still there?" she asked.

## Suburban Philadelphia Swim Club Controversy Draws State Human Rights Investigation

**HUNTINGDON VALLEY, Pa.** — A suburban Philadelphia swim club became the focus of a civil-rights controversy after a group of minority children from a day-care program said they were turned away from the club’s pool following complaints and alleged racist comments from club members.

The dispute centered on **The Valley Club**, a private swim club in Huntingdon Valley, Montgomery County, and children enrolled in **Creative Steps Inc.**, a Philadelphia day-care and summer camp program serving mostly Black and Latino children. The day-care had arranged to use the club’s pool as part of a summer outing program, but the arrangement was revoked after the children’s first visit.

### Pool Access Revoked After First Visit

Creative Steps reportedly paid for access to the swim club so dozens of children could swim there during the summer. According to the day-care and parents, the children arrived for their first visit and were met with hostility from some club patrons.

Several children and adult chaperones later said they heard racially charged remarks, including comments questioning why “Black kids” were at the pool. Some accounts alleged that white members pulled their own children from the water after the day-care children entered.

Shortly afterward, the club canceled the agreement and returned the day-care’s payment. Club representatives initially said the cancellation was due to concerns that the club could not accommodate the size of the group and that there were safety or capacity issues.

Parents and civil-rights advocates rejected that explanation, arguing that the timing of the cancellation—immediately after complaints from members and alleged racist comments—showed that the children were excluded because of race.

### Children Describe Humiliation

The episode drew national attention in part because the children involved publicly described feeling embarrassed and unwanted. Some said they believed they had been rejected because of the color of their skin.

Parents and staff members said the incident was especially painful because it involved young children who had been excited to swim during the summer. The controversy quickly moved beyond a local dispute and became a broader conversation about discrimination in private recreational spaces.

### Club Denies Racist Intent

The Valley Club denied that the decision was racially motivated. Club officials said the group was larger than expected and created operational concerns. They maintained that the cancellation was based on logistical and safety considerations, not race.

However, the club’s explanation was heavily scrutinized after reports emerged of racially offensive comments allegedly made by some members. Critics said even if club leadership framed the decision as a capacity issue, the surrounding circumstances suggested discriminatory treatment.

### Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission Opens Investigation

The **Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission (PHRC)** opened an investigation into whether the swim club violated state anti-discrimination laws. The commission examined claims that the children were denied access to a place of public accommodation because of race.

Under Pennsylvania law, businesses and certain organizations that provide services or accommodations to the public may not discriminate on the basis of race, color, religion, ancestry, national origin, sex, disability, or other protected characteristics. The legal question included whether the private swim club’s activities and paid arrangement with the day-care brought it under public-accommodation rules.

The PHRC investigation focused on the revoked contract, alleged statements made at the pool, treatment of the children compared with other guests, and the club’s stated safety and capacity justifications.

### Broader Public Response

The incident sparked outrage from civil-rights groups, elected officials, and community leaders. Demonstrations and public statements followed, with many calling the case a modern example of racial exclusion from recreational facilities—an issue with deep historical resonance in the United States.

Supporters of the children argued that the controversy recalled earlier eras when pools and clubs were used to enforce segregation. The fact that the children were from a largely minority day-care program in Philadelphia and were visiting a suburban private club intensified public debate about race, class, and access.

The case also drew media coverage across the country, turning a local pool dispute into a national civil-rights story.

### Legal and Civil-Rights Significance

The controversy raised several important questions:

- Whether a private club can revoke a paid agreement with an outside group without violating anti-discrimination law  
- Whether alleged racist comments by members can be considered evidence of discriminatory treatment  
- Whether the stated reasons of “capacity” and “safety” were legitimate or pretextual  
- How civil-rights protections apply when private clubs open facilities to nonmembers for payment  

For the families involved, the central issue was more direct: children who had been invited to swim were made to feel unwelcome and then barred from returning.

### Continuing Impact

The Valley Club controversy became one of the most widely reported discrimination cases in Pennsylvania at the time. It placed renewed attention on the role of state human-rights agencies in investigating discrimination outside traditional workplaces and housing disputes.

For the children and parents of Creative Steps, the case was not only about pool access but also about dignity, equal treatment, and the message sent to young children when they are excluded from a community space.

The PHRC investigation marked a formal effort to determine whether the club’s actions amounted to unlawful discrimination, while the public debate surrounding the case underscored how allegations of racial exclusion can rapidly become a matter of national concern.
